name: Rhododendrol

lead: Rhododendrol was a plant-derived whitening ingredient in Japanese cosmetics. Reports of patchy white skin among users led to its withdrawal in 2013.
It now appears in research as an example of how a tyrosinase inhibitor can damage the pigment cells it acts on.

paras: It inhibits tyrosinase but is also oxidized by the enzyme into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes; immune responses have also been studied.
Documented harm is leukoderma. Wikipedia reports that pigment returns in most cases after stopping, and that its use has been prohibited since 2013.

lead: Rhododendrol (RD, related to raspberry ketone) is a phenolic compound that occurs naturally in Rhododendron and other plants and was developed as a melanin-synthesis inhibitor for skin-lightening cosmetics [1][2][3]. It was used as a skin-whitening agent until July 2013, when reports emerged that users had developed patchy depigmentation (leukoderma), after which the products were withdrawn [4][3].

Subsequent research examined why a tyrosinase inhibitor produced depigmentation. Studies found that tyrosinase oxidizes rhododendrol into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes, and some work has also examined immune involvement [1][4][5][6]. It is mainly discussed today as a case study in cosmetic depigmenting-agent safety.
infobox: Phenolic tyrosinase inhibitor (former cosmetic whitening agent)

paras: Rhododendrol was described as an inhibitor of melanin synthesis developed for lightening and whitening cosmetics, and was reported to induce a depigmentary disorder principally at sites of repeated contact [1]. Researchers described the unexpected depigmentation, which showed diverse symptoms, in some subjects who used a tyrosinase-inhibiting quasi-drug containing it [7]. Wikipedia states that pigment returns in most cases after exposure stops, with spread to unexposed areas occurring only after severe damage, and notes that the knowledge of its effects is limited because of the prohibition [3].

Laboratory studies found that rhododendrol competitively inhibits mushroom tyrosinase and also serves as a substrate; it was cytotoxic to cultured human melanocytes at concentrations sufficient to inhibit tyrosinase, and the cytotoxicity was abolished by a copper chelator [1]. Oxidation by tyrosinase produces RD-quinone and then 2-methylchromane-6,7-dione, proposed as the ultimate toxic metabolite [4]. Human tyrosinase can oxidize both enantiomers of the compound [8]. A study proposed that depigmentation relates to tyrosinase activity reaching a certain threshold [7]. Reviews and studies of patients with rhododendrol-induced leukoderma have examined biochemical, cytological and immune mechanisms, including skin immunopathology and ultrastructure [5][9][6].

No studies found of clinical trials of rhododendrol as a treatment. The human data are analyses of patients who developed leukoderma after cosmetic use, such as an immune pathological and ultrastructural skin analysis of affected patients [6].

timeline.event: Developed as a tyrosinase inhibitor for lightening cosmetics, according to Wikipedia [3].
Reported to induce leukoderma in July; products withdrawn [4][3].
Studies published on the tyrosinase-dependent melanocyte toxicity mechanism [1][4].
